sentences.text: Mala lived in Tarawa, the capital of the small island nation of Kiribati, in the middle of the Pacific Ocean.
Tarawa was an atoll — a long thin curve of coral islands strung around a large shallow lagoon.
If you looked at it from a plane, it looked like a green necklace floating on the biggest blue in the world.
Maybe sixty thousand people lived along the atoll.
Mala's family was one of them.
Her father, Tavita, was a fisherman.
Her mother had died of a fever when Mala was three.
Since then Mala had been raised by her father and by her father's older sister, whom she called Aunt Teuea, who lived next door.
Mala was eleven.
She loved being on the boat with her father.
It was not always allowed — school got in the way most of the time — but on Saturdays, if the weather was good, her father sometimes took her out with him for the morning.
They would leave at dawn.
They would go out to a small reef about eight kilometers from the harbor.
They would drop nets.
They would wait.
They would come back in by noon.
Sometimes with a lot of fish, sometimes with a few.
Either way, Mala loved every minute of it.
On that particular Saturday in June it was calm and sunny.
They had gone out at five in the morning and had fished at the usual reef for maybe three hours.
They had a decent catch — enough for a good week.
Around eight they had started the motor and had begun the trip back.
That was when the motor made a strange sound.
A small cough.
Then a bigger cough.
Then it stopped.
Tavita spent maybe fifteen minutes trying to restart it.
He tried everything he knew.
He was calm — he had had a motor die before — but he was serious.
The motor was not going to restart.
He turned to Mala.
He said, "Mala.
Look.
The motor is done.
Something in it has broken.
It is not something I can fix with what I have here.
That means we cannot go back the fast way.
We have to wait."
Mala said, "Can we sail back." Their boat did have a small emergency sail — a simple square canvas that could be rigged if there was wind.
Tavita looked around.
He said, "We could try.
But the wind is going the wrong way.
It is coming from the west, and Tarawa is to the west.
We would be sailing straight into it.
That is very slow.
It would take us — many hours.
Maybe a whole day.
And the wind is picking up.
I do not want to be out on open water in a small boat if the wind gets stronger.
It is going to get stronger."
He looked around again.
He pointed at something.
Mala turned.
Maybe two kilometers away, sticking up out of the ocean, was a tiny green speck.
It was a small uninhabited atoll — one of the many small coral spits in the region.
Mala had seen it from the boat many times.
It had no name that she knew of.
Nobody lived on it.
It was just a small ring of coral with a few coconut palms and some low bushes and a small lagoon in the middle.
Tavita said, "That is where we go.
That is our island.
We sail there.
We land.
We wait.
Someone will notice we did not come back.
Aunt Teuea will notice by lunchtime today.
She will call the harbor.
The harbor will send someone to look.
It will take them a day or two, maybe.
But they will come."
It took them two hours to sail the two kilometers to the atoll.
Tavita rigged the small sail.
It caught the wind poorly — the wind was almost exactly wrong for reaching the atoll — but by tacking back and forth, and by paddling occasionally, they made progress.
The atoll got closer.
Mala could see it more clearly now.
It was tiny.
Maybe two hundred meters across at its widest.
A ring of white coral sand around a small shallow lagoon.
Maybe fifteen coconut palms.
Some low green bushes.
They landed on the western shore, on the side facing home.
Tavita pulled the boat up onto the sand.
They tied it to a coconut palm.
They stood on the beach.
Tavita looked at his watch.
He said, "It is ten in the morning.
Aunt Teuea will start to worry by two.
She will call at three.
The harbor patrol might come today, if we are lucky.
If not — tomorrow morning.
Maybe the day after.
We have food for one day.
We have water for one day.
We have the whole island.
We will be fine.
But we have to be smart.
Do you understand." Mala said, "Yes."
Tavita went to work.
He was calm and efficient.
He walked around the whole small island in about twenty minutes to see what it had.
He came back and told Mala the plan.
First — coconuts, for water.
There were plenty on the palms.
Second — driftwood, for a fire.
There was a good amount on the beaches.
Third — a small camp above the high-water mark, in the shade of the palms.
Fourth — a signal fire ready to light when they saw a boat.
Mala worked with him.
They gathered driftwood into a pile.
They knocked down four coconuts with a long stick — Tavita was patient about this, and Mala got the last one down herself, after twenty minutes of trying.
They opened them with a small hatchet Tavita had in the boat, and they drank the coconut water — sweet, cool, exactly what they needed.
They ate the small amount of food they had — two small pieces of dried fish and a small handful of rice they cooked in a tin can over a small fire.
That was lunch.
Tavita said, "For supper — we fish.
There is a reef right on the outside of the atoll.
We will catch something.
Do not worry about food.
Kiribati people have lived on islands like this for a thousand years.
Small islands are enough."
